title: Expenses, the cash book and paying yourself

say: Expenses, the cash book, and paying yourself.
This is the video for Module 3, Expenses and cash records.
An expense is any money the business pays out. There are two very different kinds. Stock purchases are goods you buy to sell again, like bags of rice or bales of fabric.

panel.heading: Where did my money go?
items: Stock purchases: goods you sell again
Running costs: everything else to keep trading
Small costs add up to a real sum

say: Running costs are everything else: transport, rent, market levy, nylon bags, phone data, a helper's pay. Keep them in separate columns.

panel.heading: Where did my money go?
items: Stock purchases: goods you sell again
Running costs: everything else to keep trading
Small costs add up to a real sum

say: Running costs look small next to stock. But if you do not record them, you will think you are making more profit than you are.

panel.heading: Where did my money go?
items: Stock purchases: goods you sell again
Running costs: everything else to keep trading
Small costs add up to a real sum

say: For example, Rukayat sells shoes at a Lagos market. Transport costs her about 1,500 naira a day for 6 days. That is 9,000 naira.
The market levy is 300 naira a day, so 1,800 naira.
Two packs of nylon bags cost 2,400 naira.
Data for WhatsApp selling is 1,500 naira, and her Saturday helper gets 3,000 naira.
Her running costs come to about 17,700 naira a week. Transport is the biggest, so she looks for a cheaper way, like sharing a keke with a neighbour trader.
Keep receipts by month, and screenshot every transfer you pay.
The cash book records every naira in and out, in date order, with a balance after each line. Step one. Count your cash and write it as the opening balance.

panel.heading: Keep a running balance
items: Write the opening balance you counted

say: Then line by line, add money in and take away money out. Today's closing balance becomes tomorrow's opening balance.

panel.heading: Keep a running balance
items: Write the opening balance you counted
panel.rule: Previous balance + money in - money out = new balance.

say: At closing, count your cash and compare. For example, Grace in Jos expected 35,000 naira but counted 34,200. She was 800 naira short.
She checked, remembered 800 naira she paid for sachet water for the shop, added the line, and the book balanced.

panel.heading: Keep a running balance
items: Write the opening balance you counted
panel.rule: Previous balance + money in - money out = new balance.

say: You cannot count bank money with your hands, so keep two sets of columns. Check cash by counting, starting each day with a fixed float of change.

panel.heading: Two columns, two checks
right: Cash to bank is not a sale

say: Check your bank or wallet balance against your app. Depositing cash at a POS agent is not a sale or an expense, just money changing pockets. But record the agent's charge as an expense.

panel.heading: Two columns, two checks
right: Cash to bank is not a sale

say: When shop money and house money share one purse, the capital slowly disappears. So think of the business as a separate person who pays you a fixed amount each week.
For example, Joy sells cooked food.

card.title: How much can Joy pay herself?

say: Her weekly sales average about 120,000 naira.

card.title: How much can Joy pay herself?

say: Ingredients cost about 72,000 naira, and gas, transport, packs and levy about 18,000.

card.title: How much can Joy pay herself?

say: So her weekly profit is about 30,000 naira.
She pays herself 20,000 naira a week and leaves 10,000 in the business to grow and cover slow weeks. If she drew 40,000, her capital would shrink.

card.title: How much can Joy pay herself?

say: Use a separate account for the business, and keep business cash in its own purse. Pay yourself on the same day each week. Write every personal withdrawal, even in an emergency, as a Drawing, not an expense.
And keep cash safe. Do not leave large amounts in the stall overnight, and do not count large sums openly in the market.

panel.heading: Separate and safe
items: A separate business account or wallet
Business cash in its own purse or box
Pay yourself on the same day each week
Write every withdrawal as a Drawing
No large cash in the stall overnight

say: To remember. Separate stock from running costs. Keep a running balance and count your cash every day. Keep cash and bank apart. Pay yourself a fixed drawing below your profit.
And each Saturday, bring your totals together on one summary page, then add the weeks into a monthly summary.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Keep a running balance and count daily
Cash and bank in separate columns
Pay yourself a fixed drawing below profit
Add weeks into a monthly summary

say: Now track one week of expenses, balance your cash book for three days, set your weekly drawing, and do your first monthly summary. Continue with the lessons below.
